record.original_question: Do there exist spherical orbifolds, meaning quotients of round spheres by finite isometry groups, that have exactly the same Laplace-Beltrami eigenvalues when multiplicities are ignored but have different Riemannian volumes?

evidence.quote: Question 1.1. Do there exist examples of eigenvalue equivalent spherical orbifolds whose volumes differ?
In Section 3 we will answer this question in the affirmative in every dimension n ≥ 9 by proving the following theorem.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
A spherical orbifold is a quotient $S^n/\Gamma$ of the round $n$-sphere $S^n$ (with its standard constant-curvature-$1$ Riemannian metric) by a finite subgroup $\Gamma$ of the isometry group $O(n+1)$, equipped with the induced Riemannian orbifold structure. The Laplace–Beltrami operator on such an orbifold has a discrete spectrum consisting of nonnegative real eigenvalues, each occurring with finite multiplicity. Call two spherical orbifolds eigenvalue equivalent if the underlying sets of distinct Laplace eigenvalues coincide (i.e., they have identical spectra after multiplicities are ignored). The Riemannian volume of $S^n/\Gamma$ is $\mathrm{vol}(S^n)/|\Gamma|$.

Question: Do there exist two spherical orbifolds (in some dimension $n$) that are eigenvalue equivalent in the above sense but have different Riemannian volumes?
artifact.status_search_result: The question is answered affirmatively in every dimension $n \geq 9$ via an explicit construction, while the analogous question in low dimensions appears to remain unresolved.

status_evidence.title: The spectral geometry of hyperbolic and spherical manifolds: analogies and open problems
